Can you put together a short doc or point us to the DPA clauses that cover these? We’d like to close on this during legal review next week.

Rishi / team / Daniel — quick legal read below. I pulled relevant excerpts into the attached DPA and exported our current subprocessors list. High-level responses:

1) BYOK / Customer-controlled keys
- Our standard Private deployment supports Bring-Your-Own-Key (BYOK) via customer-managed KMS. Redwood supports key wrapping and envelope encryption models; we do not retain key material. DPA clause 4.2 (Encryption & Keys) clarifies customer control and key destruction on deprovision.
- Operational note: for on-prem installs where the customer supplies an HSM, Redwood services authenticate to endpoints but cannot extract raw key material from the HSM.

2) Access to plaintext / operator access
- For VPC and on-prem modes, the default model is that customer data remains within customer-controlled networks. Redwood’s control plane (for Private) operates in a management channel; by default, we do not have administrative access to customer plaintext. DPA clause 5.1 (Access Controls) enumerates the limited exceptions (e.g., emergency bugfix with customer-approved ephemeral access, or court order) and requires prior notice and audit logging.

3) Subprocessors
- Attached is the current subprocessors list (export). Our policy: we notify customers 30 days in advance for non-critical additions and provide options for objection or mitigation. Critical security patches may be deployed with shorter notice for emergency risk.

4) Cross-border transfers
- If telemetry (health/metrics) is configured to be sent to Redwood, customer can select regional telemetry endpoints. For EU customers, we support SCCs and can route telemetry to EU regions. DPA section 7 covers international transfers and safeguards.

Next steps:
- Monica / Priyom: please add a short technical appendix describing the exact TLS/KMS integrations and where logs are stored by default vs. optional routing.
- Rishi: propose a 30-minute call with Daniel and their legal/security team next week to walk through the DPA changes.

I’ll also add a redline view to the DocuSign link Lauren will circulate.

Lauren Bishop
Senior Counsel, Contracts & Privacy | Redwood Inference

Daniel — thanks for the specific questions. Below are concise technical answers we can include in the appendix or the SOW:

1) KV / Model cache behavior
- Model KV cache: in Redwood Private when using customer-managed hosts, the KV cache is held in RAM on the inference nodes. If BYOK is enabled, tokens are encrypted at-rest and in transit; however, during inference some data is materialized in memory for computation.
- Controls: we support node-level encryption (dm-crypt) and FIPS-certified HSM integrations for key operations, role-based access controls (RBAC), and full audit logging of operator sessions. By default, engineer access to nodes is restricted to escalation-only channels and requires documented approval; all such access is audited and time-limited.

2) Management channel topology
- Two main options: (a) private peering/VPN where the control-plane API connects over an encrypted peer to customer VPC, or (b) HTTPS-based control plane over public Internet using mutual TLS and customer IP allowlists. For highest assurance, customers choose private peering and limit egress.

3) Subprocessor objections / mitigations
- Practical options: (a) technical mitigation — we can route telemetry to an alternative regional endpoint that does not touch the new subprocessor, (b) contractual mitigation — add a narrow restriction in the DPA for that subprocessor, or (c) commercial — carve-out exception negotiated in the contract. Termination is last resort.

I’ve attached an architecture diagram that shows data and control plane flows for VPC and on-prem options. Happy to walk through on the call and annotate per Acme’s requirements.

Attachments: private_deployment_arch_diagram.png

Regards,
